verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Dewas engineering units with funded order books and tight monthly cash discipline; avoid firecracker-adjacent and thin-margin fabrication units until local GST trend turns.
title: Dewas Engineering & Capital Goods: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Dewas engineering units convert steel, tube and castings into fabricated structures, precision tubes and machined parts, and cash comes back only after dispatch, inspection and retention release.** The value sits in the order book and the customer relationship, not the machine; the cash sits in receivables and work-in-progress, which is why the working capital cycle is the real credit risk [9][11]. **Capex is lumpy and order-led, so a proposal for a new line must be matched to a signed order, not to a forecast.** For EPC-type work the cash conversion cycle runs longer than for OEMs because execution periods stretch [11], so when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower is an OEM or an EPC supplier; if EPC, ask for the milestone-wise billing schedule and retention terms. ## What has changed now
**The national demand signal is strong but the local tax signal is not.** India-wide IIP for NIC 28 is +10.3% YoY and +10.4% Apr-to-date [D], and exports are +19.8% Apr-to-date in USD [D]. Against that, Madhya Pradesh GST collections are -0.1% Apr-to-date versus India +6.1%, 6.2 pp slower [D]. **So when a Dewas proposal lands, check the borrower's own GST returns against the state trend; if his filings are flat while he claims order growth, ask for the buyer-wise sales register.** Local sources are thin on this city's engineering cluster, so lean on first principles and peers. Note the local firecracker factory blast of May 2026 [1] — it is not engineering, but it tells you safety and licence compliance in Dewas industrial premises get scrutiny; verify factory licence and safety records for any unit handling volatile inputs. ## Where the growth is
**Pursue precision-tube and machined-component suppliers feeding data-centre, mining, off-highway and railway customers, and piping/fittings units tied to oil and gas.** Peer evidence supports this: Pitti cites data-centre power needs and global sourcing consolidation as structural demand [4]; DEE's piping and fittings order book crossed Rs 1,300 crore with Q3 revenue up 77% YoY to ₹286.7 crore [5]; Skipper reported its highest-ever Q2 revenue with PAT up 56% [6]. **Avoid pure fabrication job-work units with single customers and no retention history, and avoid anyone whose margin depends on one buyer's price revision.** Suzlon shows volume growth without margin — revenue up 26% to Rs 4,869 crore but EBITDA margin down to 14.8% from 18.6% [7] — so when a proposal lands, check whether volume growth is coming with falling margin; if yes, ask for the price-variation clause in the contract. ## How to grow safely
**Structure every limit against the order book, not the balance sheet.** Take monthly: GST returns, buyer-wise sales and receivable ageing, order book with delivery dates, and stock statement reconciled to WIP. ## Early-warning signs
**Watch receivable days crossing the contract retention period, WIP rising faster than billing, and GST filings turning flat while order book grows.** If any two appear together, freeze enhancement and re-price.
watch: borrower filings flat while MP stays at -0.1% [D] -> ask for buyer-wise sales register and hold enhancement
receivable days exceed retention period -> re-price limit and seek additional collateral
WIP rises faster than billing for two quarters -> freeze limit and inspect site
volume up but margin down, as with Suzlon 14.8% vs 18.6% [7] -> ask for price-variation clause and re-cut limit
